This matters because Japan did not build its Indian position through one agreement alone. It built it through accumulated presence. Industrial cooperation, manufacturing, supplier training, local employment, research and development, quality systems, patient capital and repeated government-business dialogue all played a role. Japan has also increased its administrative and diplomatic attention to India. The creation of a dedicated Japan-India Economic Affairs Division by the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs underlines how seriously Tokyo now treats the economic relationship with New Delhi. India is not just another market file. It is becoming a strategic economic file in its own right. Europe should pay attention. The EU has strong trade negotiators and excellent regulatory capacity, but business follow-through is often fragmented between EU institutions, Member States, chambers of commerce, regional agencies, private consultants and sector bodies. India does not need another European brochure. It needs European continuity. 나렌드라 모디 인도 총리와 스즈키자동차 오사무 스즈키 회장이 2022년 8월 인도 간디나가르에서 열린 스즈키 마루티의 인도 파트너십 40주년 기념 행사에서 손을 흔들고 있다. (출처: 뉴시스) The Suzuki lesson: localisation is not a slogan At India Salon Brussels, participants referred to examples such as Maruti Suzuki and Toyota to show that successful business in India requires more than selling into India. It requires adjusting to India. The Suzuki story is powerful because it shows how a foreign company can become local without disappearing into the local market. Maruti Suzuki did not simply import Japanese cars. It worked with Indian conditions, Indian roads, Indian consumers, Indian price sensitivity and Indian industrial development. The result was a brand that helped shape India’s mass automobile market. In 2022, Maruti Suzuki commemorated 40 years of Suzuki’s partnership with India. During that ceremony, Suzuki announced a new R&D centre in India, intended to strengthen research capabilities for India and global markets. That is not just production. That is knowledge transfer, engineering, talent development and confidence in Indian technical capacity. Europe should draw a direct lesson from this. If European companies only see India as a place to sell finished products, they will remain vulnerable. If they see India as a place to design, test, adapt, produce and scale, their position changes. India is not only a demand market. It is also an innovation market. It has engineers, software developers, industrial clusters, family businesses, skilled technicians, agricultural knowledge, pharmaceutical capacity, textile traditions, digital public infrastructure and a population that can test products at enormous scale. A European product that works in India may later work in Africa, Southeast Asia, the Middle East or Latin America. A European product that cannot survive India’s price sensitivity, infrastructure gaps, climatic conditions and regional diversity may not be as globally competitive as its maker believes. Korea understood speed, scale and consumer intimacy South Korea followed a different path from Japan, but its lesson is equally important. Korean companies often combine rapid execution with heavy localisation, strong branding and aggressive consumer proximity. Samsung, Hyundai and LG are not marginal players in India. They are deeply visible in daily life: mobile phones, televisions, refrigerators, cars, service centres, showrooms and advertising. They did not become familiar to Indian consumers by waiting for perfect market conditions. They invested, expanded, adapted and kept selling. Samsung’s Noida factory is a clear symbol of this approach. The factory, set up in 1996, became one of Samsung’s key electronics manufacturing facilities in India. In 2018, Samsung inaugurated a major expansion and described the Noida plant as the world’s largest mobile factory, with capacity planned to double from 68 million to 120 million mobile phones a year. Samsung also stressed that it had entered India in 1995 and built factories, R&D centres, a design centre, retail networks and customer service points across the country. That is not remote exporting. That is industrial occupation in the positive economic sense: being physically present, visible, accessible and accountable. Hyundai offers another lesson. Hyundai entered India in 1996 and has since developed India into one of its major global manufacturing and export bases. Its more recent investment plans show that India is no longer viewed merely as an emerging consumer market, but as a production, research and export hub. Europe should not copy Korea blindly. But it should understand the strategic principle. Korea does not only ask how to export to India. Korea asks how to become part of India’s consumption, production and service landscape. The Korean CEPA lesson: agreements need industrial follow-up India and South Korea already have their own Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. It came into effect in 2010 and covers trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights and investment. India and Korea have continued to discuss improvements and updates, including goods, services, rules of origin, investment and sanitary and phytosanitary standards. This is important for Europe because it shows that trade agreements are not static trophies. They need maintenance. They create disputes. They expose imbalances. They require review, sectoral correction and political patience. The EU-India agreement will be no different. European companies should not imagine that once the agreement enters into force, India will suddenly become easy. There will still be customs questions, certification questions, data questions, sustainability questions, labour questions, regional differences and administrative friction. Korean companies did not avoid all of that. They built through it. Europe must do the same. It must prepare companies not only to enter India, but to survive the second, third and fourth year. The first year is often curiosity. The later years reveal whether the strategy is real. 2024년 9월 24일 인도 첸나이 외곽 스리페룸부두르에 있는 삼성 공장. (출처: 뉴시스) Europe is strong in rules, but India asks for relationships Europe’s great strength is regulation. The EU can set standards that reach far beyond its borders because access to the European market requires compliance with European rules. That was also discussed at India Salon Brussels. Sustainability, reporting, traceability, pesticide residues, green claims, supply-chain documentation and labour conditions are now part of trade reality. This gives Europe power. But it can also create arrogance. For Indian businesses, Europe can look like a maze of standards, audits, certificates and slow replies. For European businesses, India can look unpredictable, informal and difficult to read. Both perceptions contain some truth. But neither is sufficient. Japan and Korea show that companies succeed when they translate rules into relationships. They build local teams that understand the administration. They create service networks that understand the consumer. They train suppliers. They invest in people who can move between headquarters and Indian realities. They accept that India cannot be reduced to one national operating model. The EU-India agreement contains opportunities for exporters, service providers, investors, agricultural producers, technology firms and industrial manufacturers. But even the best agreement will not replace trust. A reduced tariff can open a door. It cannot build a market. India is federal, regional and deeply diverse One of the recurring points in the Brussels discussion was that India is not one single market. That sentence is often repeated, but not always taken seriously. India’s states differ in language, infrastructure, political culture, food habits, consumer behaviour, purchasing power, industrial policy, labour availability and administrative practice. A European company that enters Maharashtra may have a very different experience from one that enters Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala or West Bengal. Japan and Korea often learned this through physical presence. Their companies built plants in specific locations, developed regional supplier bases and adapted products to local expectations. Europe often starts from a macro-view: India as one country, one market, one growth story. That is too abstract. Europe must learn to choose India state by state, sector by sector and partner by partner. This is especially important for small and medium-sized European companies. A large multinational can absorb mistakes. An SME cannot. For many European SMEs, India should not begin with a national strategy. It should begin with one state, one reliable partner, one product, one compliance pathway and one clear customer segment. That may sound modest. In India, it is often the only serious way to start. The after-sales lesson European companies often underestimate after-sales service in India. They focus on product quality, technology and brand reputation. But in India, service accessibility can decide whether a product survives. Korean consumer brands understood this very well. Samsung’s communication about India stressed not only manufacturing, but also retail outlets and customer service points across the country. That is a business lesson, not a marketing detail. In a market as large and varied as India, trust is built after the sale. Can the product be repaired? Is there a local contact? Are spare parts available? Does the warranty mean something? Does the company answer? Is the brand visible in smaller cities? Can the family trust it? Can the business buyer rely on it when something breaks? European companies that enter India with premium products but weak service networks risk becoming niche suppliers for a small urban elite. That may be profitable in some sectors, but it is not an India strategy. Japan and Korea often built networks before Europe finished analysing risk. Local management is not optional Another lesson from Japan and Korea is the role of local management. European companies often send expatriates to India with limited preparation, limited family support and limited authority. They expect them to “manage India” while key decisions remain in Europe. That rarely works. India requires local decision-making. It also requires trust in Indian managers. Companies that keep India as a subordinate sales territory will not understand the speed of the market. Companies that allow Indian leadership to shape product, pricing, distribution, hiring and communication stand a much better chance. Hyundai’s appointment of Tarun Garg as the first Indian CEO of Hyundai Motor India was symbolically important in this regard. It showed that a long-established foreign company in India can move from expatriate-led presence to deeper local leadership. Europe should take that seriously. If European firms want India to become central to their global growth, Indian executives must be central to their decision-making. India’s middle class is not Europe’s middle class One of the traps for European companies is to misread India’s consumer base. India has wealth, aspiration and a rapidly changing urban economy. But it also has extreme price sensitivity, uneven income growth and enormous differences between metropolitan consumers and smaller-town or rural consumers. Japanese and Korean companies often adapted to this reality by offering products designed for Indian price points, Indian family use and Indian infrastructure conditions. This does not mean lowering quality. It means redesigning value. Europe sometimes struggles with this. A European company may think its brand justifies a premium. In India, that premium must be earned daily. Consumers may respect European quality, but they will still compare price, service, durability, availability and social proof. The Indian consumer is not waiting passively for Europe. The Indian consumer already has Indian, Korean, Japanese, American and Chinese options. In many sectors, Europe is arriving late. Sustainability must become practical The India Salon debate also showed that sustainability is becoming one of the main gateways to the European market. This is not limited to large corporations. Smaller suppliers can be pulled into reporting requirements because their larger clients need data on emissions, origins, labour conditions and environmental impact. For Indian exporters, this is difficult but also strategic. A company that can document its chain, prove its claims, manage residues, trace inputs and verify labour practices can gain an advantage in Europe. A company that treats sustainability as marketing language will face growing risk. Europe can help here, but only if it avoids preaching. Indian producers need practical pathways: affordable certification, clear documentation, cooperative training, technology transfer, testing capacity and predictable demand. The question is not whether European standards matter. They do. The question is whether Europe can help partners meet them without turning compliance into a wall. Japan and Korea are useful examples because they often think in ecosystems. They train suppliers. They build industrial clusters. They support quality improvement. Europe must bring the same ecosystem thinking to sustainability. Agriculture will test the agreement Agriculture was one of the most concrete parts of the Brussels discussion. Mangoes, spices, moringa, natural farming, organic products, pesticide residues and traceability all came up. The lesson was simple: a product may be attractive, but access to Europe depends on the chain behind it. This is where the EU-India agreement will face real-world pressure. Europe wants safe food, credible green claims and protection for sensitive sectors. India wants opportunity for its producers, farmers and exporters. Both positions are legitimate. But a trade agreement will only work if it creates practical bridges between them. If an Indian producer wants to sell organic or residue-free products to Europe, the surrounding farming environment may matter. If neighbouring fields use pesticides, contamination risks may arise. That means export readiness is not only an individual company issue. It can become a village, district or regional organisation issue. Europe should not underestimate this. It should work with India on testing infrastructure, farmer training, cooperative models, local incentives and traceability tools. Otherwise, agricultural opportunity will remain limited to a small number of well-organised exporters. Moringa as a practical example During the Brussels discussion, moringa became one of the most concrete examples of how European market access works in practice. A producer who wants to bring moringa to Europe cannot only focus on yield, packaging or price. The product must also be documented, tested and credible. If it is presented as organic or residue-free, the production environment must support that claim. That means the farmer’s own field is not enough. The wider area matters. If neighbouring farms use pesticides, contamination risks can remain. If water sources are polluted, that can affect the product. If transport, storage or processing are poorly documented, the commercial story weakens. This is where trade becomes local development. To export to Europe, a producer may need to convince neighbouring farmers, organise training, create common standards, invest in testing, build traceability and secure better prices. A European customer buying moringa may therefore be influencing not only one producer, but an entire farming zone. That is the kind of practical economic cooperation that the EU-India agreement should support. Natural farming and new rural income The discussion also touched on natural farming, soil quality, water protection and possible additional income streams for rural areas. Hemp was mentioned as a plant with deep roots that can store carbon in the soil and may also help in the context of polluted land. The idea of certified carbon storage as a possible source of income was discussed, alongside broader questions about natural methods and environmental restoration. There were also ideas about microplastics in water and possible natural techniques to bind or address them. Such ideas require further study and verification, but their presence in the discussion showed that EU-India cooperation does not need to be limited to export volumes. It can also involve agricultural knowledge, soil restoration, water quality, biodiversity and rural development. This is another area where Europe can learn from India. India has centuries of agricultural knowledge, local experimentation and low-cost adaptation. Europe has strong scientific institutions, regulatory systems and market demand for verifiable sustainability. If these strengths are combined correctly, the result can be more than trade. It can become applied cooperation. Labour mobility is also trade policy At India Salon Brussels, labour mobility was not treated as a separate migration issue. It was part of the economic conversation. That is the right approach. Trade is not only goods crossing borders. It is people building confidence. Indian professionals in Europe can help European companies understand India. European entrepreneurs in India can help build new partnerships. Students, engineers, technicians, advisers and families become part of the bridge. Japan and Korea have used people, training and company culture as part of their India strategy. Europe must do the same, but in a way that respects rights, family life and social protection. Belgium and other European countries face labour shortages in several sectors. India has skills, ambition and a young workforce. But mobility must not become exploitation. If Europe wants Indian talent, it must offer clear rules, fair treatment and real inclusion. Otherwise, it will lose credibility. The same applies in reverse. European companies sending people to India must prepare them properly. India is not only different in the office. It is different in housing, schooling, traffic, family expectations, bureaucracy, food, climate, social rhythm and support networks. Failed expatriation is not always a business failure. Often it is a family failure that the company failed to anticipate. Culture also determines whether trade works The Brussels meeting repeatedly moved beyond tariffs and rules. Cultural differences were seen as at least as important. India and Europe were discussed as two large civilisational spaces with long histories, many languages, regional differences and strong internal diversity. India was not viewed only as a nation state, but also as a society with deep historical layers, religious influences, family networks and local identities. Europe also has its own cultural and political history, shaped by humanism, individual rights, privacy, the rule of law and regulation. This comparison helped clarify that companies do not only exchange products. They also bring expectations with them. If those expectations are not understood, misunderstandings become more likely. One cultural contribution focused on the difference between the European emphasis on the individual and the Indian emphasis on embedded responsibility. The concept of dharma was used to describe how a person in India is often seen within a wider web of obligations towards family, profession, country and society. This differs from the European tradition, where individual rights, personal choice, privacy and autonomy are more central. These differences do not have to block cooperation, but they must be understood. They can influence business decisions, loyalty, negotiation, risk-taking, family choices and the way people relate to institutions. Expatriates do not fail only in the office The cultural discussion became very practical when participants spoke about expatriates and entrepreneurs moving to India. It was noted that foreign entrepreneurs or employees may leave India again within a few years if cultural and family realities weigh more heavily than expected. The difficulties do not arise only in meetings or offices. They also emerge in housing, schools, the role of spouses, services, traffic, social habits and the search for a support network. Spouses of posted employees can face particular difficulties when they have no clear work rights or personal role. The conclusion was that companies should not wait until after arrival to provide support. Intercultural training, family guidance and realistic information about living in India should be organised beforehand. Here again, Japan and Korea offer lessons. Companies that build long-term international careers must think beyond the contract. They must think about families, schools, language, health care, local adaptation and emotional resilience. A failed posting can destroy a market strategy. A well-supported posting can create a bridge for decades. Europe must stop confusing caution with strategy European companies are often cautious. In some sectors, caution is justified. India can be difficult. Legal processes can be slow. Infrastructure can vary. Regulation can change. Partners must be checked carefully. Payment risk, intellectual property concerns and administrative delays are real. But caution is not a strategy. Japan and Korea did not succeed in India because they were reckless. They succeeded because they converted caution into structure. They built local companies, trained people, developed networks, negotiated with authorities, invested in plants and stayed long enough to learn. Europe must move from hesitation to structured commitment. That means sector-specific India desks, not occasional trade missions. It means India-capable management, not only export managers. It means local legal, tax and cultural advice before market entry, not after the first dispute. It means building with Indian partners instead of treating them only as distributors. It means board-level patience. India is not a quarter-by-quarter market. It is a decade-by-decade market. Skills as an economic asset India was also discussed as a country where many technical and artisanal skills remain strong. In Europe, some skills have weakened or disappeared because of industrialisation, outsourcing and changing labour markets. Textiles, khadi, natural dyes, agriculture, food processing, digital services and artisanal production were mentioned as fields where India has knowledge that can be valuable for Europe. At the same time, that knowledge must be translated into documentation, certification and quality standards that European customers understand. The challenge is therefore not only to produce, but also to prove, explain and deliver consistently. This is where Europe and India can complement each other. Europe can bring standardisation, testing, quality frameworks, consumer trust and regulatory clarity. India can bring craft, flexibility, scale, entrepreneurial speed and production knowledge. The mistake would be to think that one side must teach and the other side must learn. The more realistic conclusion is that both sides have serious lessons to absorb. ⓒ천지일보 2026.07.06. (챗GPT) Young people, training and social progress The discussion also touched on the role of training and skills development in India. Participants referred to programmes that guide young people through vocational training and into employment. Such initiatives can connect young people with Indian and international companies and allow them to grow through practical experience. This was placed within a broader discussion about social progress, rural incomes, agriculture and the question of how trade ultimately reaches ordinary people. Economic growth was not reduced to company profit. Participants raised the question of whether agreements also lead to jobs, better incomes and opportunities outside major cities. That is essential. If the EU-India agreement is only useful to large corporations, it will not create the social legitimacy it needs. If it helps farmers, SMEs, young workers, technicians, women entrepreneurs, rural communities and regional companies, it can become much more than a diplomatic success. Villages as an alternative to megacities One notable example concerned the creation of technology jobs in villages. The idea is to bring work to rural areas instead of forcing people to move to large urban centres. Bangalore was mentioned as a city that grew extremely quickly because of job concentration, creating pressure on housing, infrastructure and mobility. Village-based knowledge work was discussed as a way to reduce pressure on megacities while allowing families to remain closer to their social networks. This idea links with the broader Indian social fabric, in which family, care for older generations and shared responsibility play an important role. Europe should listen carefully to that discussion. European economic thinking often assumes that modernisation means urban concentration. India may offer another model: digital work, regional training, rural talent, local family structures and distributed opportunity. That does not mean romanticising village life. It means recognising that development does not have to copy Europe’s industrial path. Europe can also learn from India The Brussels meeting was not only about how India must adapt to Europe. It also raised the question of what Europe can learn from India. India has experience in dealing with scale, many languages, regional differences, informal networks, family businesses, entrepreneurship under pressure and rapid adaptation. Europe is strong in rules, consumer protection, human rights, privacy, product standards and institutional procedures. The challenge is to bring these strengths together. India can benefit from European clarity on standards. Europe can learn from Indian flexibility, entrepreneurship and the capacity to operate in highly diverse conditions. This is also where Korea and Japan become useful reference points. They did not enter India by pretending India was easy. They entered by accepting India’s difficulty as part of the business model. European companies should do the same. India is not a market for companies that need perfect predictability before moving. It is a market for companies that can prepare well, adapt fast and remain serious. Students and public perception Public perception came back in the discussion about students and media. It was noted that European students often raise critical questions about labour conditions, wages and human rights in India, while also buying low-cost fashion in European stores. That tension shows how difficult the debate on trade can be. Consumers want ethical production, but low prices remain attractive. By bringing students, entrepreneurs and speakers into direct contact, a more balanced view may emerge. The aim is not to remove criticism, but to make the discussion more honest. Trade can only be discussed fairly when both sides also examine their own role. Travel, business visits and direct contact with local entrepreneurs were seen as ways to reduce stereotypes. That is important because outdated European images of India still influence business decisions. India is too often viewed through poverty, outsourcing or low-cost production. That image is incomplete and increasingly misleading. India is also a space programme, a digital infrastructure laboratory, a pharmaceutical power, a services giant, a manufacturing contender, an agricultural civilisation and a consumer market in transformation. Europe needs a more adult view of India. The role of Brussels The choice of Brussels was not accidental. The city is close to the European Commission, the European Parliament, trade representations, diplomatic networks, business federations and international advisory circles. India Salon Brussels wants to use that position to discuss not only the agreement itself, but also the practical steps needed to make cooperation work. During the opening part of the event, the importance of links with the European institutions was clearly underlined. The EU-India agreement does not stand apart from regulation, sustainability policy, labour market questions, investment rules and the way Europe projects economic influence. For Indian companies, Brussels is not only the capital of Belgium. It is also a place where rules are prepared that later shape access to the European market. For European companies, Brussels is a place where they can better understand how India is changing as a market, partner and production base. That makes Brussels a useful meeting point, but not the end point. The discussion must travel from Brussels to Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Pune, Delhi, Kolkata and many other centres of Indian economic life. EICBI as institutional partner The Europe India Center for Business and Industry was the institutional partner of India Salon Brussels. Its involvement gave the gathering a clear business and policy dimension. The room brought together people with experience in chambers of commerce, export, import, public policy, technology, diplomacy, research, business networks and market-entry advice. This made the conversation broad. No single sector dominated the event. The same question returned from different angles: how can European and Indian companies understand each other faster without underestimating legal, cultural and practical challenges? That question is precisely where Europe must become more serious. The answer will not come only from EU negotiators. It will come from entrepreneurs, farmers, engineers, lawyers, customs experts, students, family businesses, industrial groups, labour specialists, sustainability auditors, local governments and people willing to work across cultures. Joris Hindryckx as a notable guest at the European Parliament Earlier on Tuesday 9 June 2026, a meeting also took place in the morning at the European Parliament, where the broader cooperation between Europe and India had already been discussed before the India Salon Brussels gathering. Joris Hindryckx, alderman from Houthulst, was a notable guest at that morning meeting. His presence gave the day a clear West Flemish link within a discussion that mainly focused on international cooperation, economic exchange and the growing strategic importance of EU-India relations. His attendance fitted into a day on which European and Indian partners discussed their relationship at different levels. At the European Parliament, the focus was mainly on the policy context in which the Comprehensive Free Trade Agreement between the European Union and India is taking shape. That agreement is not only a trade file. It is also a framework for investment, sustainable production, knowledge exchange, labour mobility and stronger mutual market access. For Joris Hindryckx, the morning meeting placed a local representative in an environment where local, European and international interests intersect. As alderman from Houthulst, he was present in a setting where major economic and geopolitical questions were discussed, but also where the practical question arose of how European regions, entrepreneurs and local networks can respond to new forms of cooperation with India. His presence showed that the EU-India debate is not limited to capitals, diplomatic services or large companies. It is also relevant for local officeholders and regional actors who want to turn international contacts into concrete opportunities. The morning meeting at the European Parliament gave an additional institutional dimension to the conversations that continued later in the day at India Salon Brussels in Novotel Brussels Off Grand Place. Where the European Parliament meeting was connected to the institutional and political context of EU-India cooperation, the later gathering offered space for a more practical conversation between entrepreneurs, experts and participants from the broader Europe-India network. The presence of Joris Hindryckx was therefore a striking bridge between local government, European decision-making and international dialogue. Not only tariffs The core message of the meeting was that the EU-India Free Trade Agreement should not be reduced to tariff reduction. Tariffs matter, but they are only one part of market access. A company may benefit from lower duties and still get stuck on residue rules, labelling, traceability, sustainability claims, financing, cultural differences or slow decision-making. At the same time, a company with strong documentation, good relationships and reliable product quality can turn European strictness into an advantage. For Indian exporters, Europe can be a difficult but valuable market. For European companies, India can be a huge and fast-changing market, but only if they are willing to adapt their approach. That is where the comparison with Japan and Korea becomes so relevant. Their strongest companies did not treat market access as a legal event. They treated it as a long-term business operation. Europe must do the same. What the EU can learn from Japan and Korea The lesson from Japan is patience, industrial discipline and long-term institutional follow-up. The lesson from Korea is speed, consumer closeness and the courage to scale. Europe needs both. From Japan, Europe can learn to think in 30-year relationships rather than short market cycles. It can learn to invest in local production, supplier development, R&D and patient trust. It can learn that India rewards companies that adapt without losing their own strengths. From Korea, Europe can learn that brand familiarity matters, service networks matter and fast execution matters. It can learn that India’s consumers cannot be approached only through premium assumptions. They must be served, answered and understood. From both, Europe can learn that India is not “entered” once. It is entered every day. The Brussels message beneath the trade file The value of India Salon Brussels was that it brought the EU-India agreement down from institutional language to business reality. Yes, tariffs matter. Yes, sustainability matters. Yes, intellectual property, investment protection, procurement, services and customs procedures matter. But the real issue is whether companies can use the agreement. If European companies do not understand India, the agreement will remain underused. If Indian companies do not understand Europe, the agreement will become frustrating. If both sides reduce the relationship to legal texts, they will miss the human and business work required underneath. That is why Korea and Japan matter in this debate. They show that India rewards commitment. They show that adaptation is not weakness. They show that local presence can become global strength. They show that a company can begin as foreign and become trusted. An agreement with human consequences In Brussels, the Comprehensive Free Trade Agreement was ultimately discussed as something that goes far beyond figures. It concerns farmers who may need to change production methods, entrepreneurs who must learn European certification, workers looking for opportunities, families moving across borders, students adjusting their view of India, Belgian companies trying to understand India better and Indian companies learning that Europe cannot be treated as one simple market. The value of India Salon Brussels lay in that practical layer beneath the major political story. The agreement can open new trade flows, but the real test will be whether people are able to implement it. That is why this debate should not be left only to diplomats and trade lawyers. It belongs also to companies, local governments, family businesses, farmers, universities, chambers of commerce, labour organisations and civil society. Trade is not only about what crosses a border. It is also about who understands whom once the border has been crossed. Europe’s choice Europe now has a choice. It can celebrate the EU-India agreement as a diplomatic success and then leave companies to find their own way through India’s vast and demanding market. Or it can treat the agreement as the beginning of a much deeper economic learning process. The first option will produce press releases. The second may produce factories, jobs, research partnerships, cleaner supply chains, stronger SMEs, better agricultural cooperation, services growth and a more balanced relationship with India. Europe should not go to India only to sell. It should go to India to learn, build and stay. That was the deeper business lesson from India Salon Brussels. India does not need Europe to arrive with lectures. It needs Europe to arrive with seriousness. Japan and Korea have already shown part of the way. Now Europe has to decide whether it wants to visit India, or finally land there.

item.title: [세계의 창] 유럽, 인도와 교역하려면 인도에 착륙하는 법 배워야(下)
item.content:encoded: ※ 편집자 주 : 유럽연합(EU)과 인도의 포괄적 자유무역협정(CEPA) 논의는 관세와 시장 개방을 넘어 양측이 서로를 얼마나 깊이 이해하고 실제 협력으로 옮길 수 있는지를 묻고 있다. 이번 글은 유럽의 금융·규제 시스템을 20년간 취재해 온 탐사보도 기자 앤디 베르마우트가 벨기에 브뤼셀에서 열린 ‘인디아 살롱 브뤼셀’에 참석한 뒤 정리한 글의 마지막 편이다. 상편과 중편이 한국·일본 기업의 인도 진출 방식, 사후서비스, 현지 경영, 지속가능성, 농업 협력 등 실무 과제를 짚었다면 하편은 한 걸음 더 나아가 EU-인도 협정의 의미를 사람과 지역, 문화, 인식의 문제로 확장한다. 그는 EU-인도 협정이 단순한 외교적 성과나 관세 인하의 문제가 아니라고 본다. 협정의 진짜 성패는 기업과 농민, 노동자, 학생, 지역사회가 이를 어떻게 실행하고 서로를 이해하느냐에 달려 있다는 것이다. 마지막 편은 유럽이 인도를 ‘방문할 시장’이 아니라 ‘배우고 머물며 함께 구축할 공간’으로 바라봐야 한다는 메시지로 마무리된다. 앤디 버마웃. ⓒ천지일보 2025.08.17. EU-인도 협정, 관세 이상 확장해야 결국 사람, 지역, 문화, 인식의 문제 韓日 기업처럼 현지화·신뢰 구축 필요   유럽, 인도를 여전히 빈곤국으로 봐 인도는 다양성·유연성 배울 파트너 현지서 배우고 머물며 함께 구축해야 ◆거대도시의 대안으로서의 마을 브뤼셀 회의에서 주목할 만한 한 사례는 마을에 기술 관련 일자리를 만드는 것과 관련됐다. 이 아이디어는 사람들이 대도시로 이동하도록 강요하는 대신 농촌 지역으로 일을 가져오는 것을 목표로 한다. 방갈로르는 일자리 집중 때문에 매우 빠르게 성장한 도시로 언급됐고 이로 인해 주택, 인프라, 교통에 대한 압박이 가중됐다. 마을 기반 지식 노동은 가족들이 사회적 네트워크에 더 가까이 머물 수 있게 하면서 거대도시의 압박을 줄이는 방법으로 논의됐다. 이 아이디어는 가족, 노년층 돌봄, 공유된 책임이 중요한 역할을 하는 더 넓은 인도의 사회적 구조와 연결된다. 유럽의 경제 사고방식은 종종 현대화가 도시 집중을 의미한다고 가정한다. 인도는 또 다른 모델을 제시할 수 있다. 디지털 업무, 지역 훈련, 농촌 인재, 지역 가족 구조, 분산된 기회다. 이는 마을 생활을 낭만적으로 미화하자는 게 아니다. 개발이 반드시 유럽의 산업화 경로를 따라야만 하는 것은 아니라는 점을 인식하자는 의미다. ◆유럽도 인도에서 배울 수 있다 브뤼셀 회의는 인도가 유럽에 어떻게 적응해야 하는가에 관한 것만이 아니었다. 그것은 유럽이 인도에서 무엇을 배울 수 있는가라는 질문도 제기했다. 인도는 대규모 운영, 다양한 언어, 지역적 차이, 비공식 네트워크, 가족 기업, 압박 속의 기업가 정신, 빠른 적응을 다루는 경험이 있다. 유럽은 규칙, 소비자 보호, 인권, 사생활, 제품 기준, 제도적 절차에 강하다. 과제는 이 강점들을 함께 가져오는 것이다. 인도는 기준에 관한 유럽의 명확성에서 이익을 얻을 수 있다. 유럽은 인도의 유연성, 기업가 정신, 매우 다양한 조건에서 작동하는 능력에서 배울 수 있다. 바로 여기서 한국과 일본은 유용한 참고점이 된다. 그들은 인도가 쉽다고 가장하면서 인도에 진입하지 않았다. 그들은 인도의 어려움을 사업 모델의 일부로 받아들이며 진입했다. 유럽 기업들도 그렇게 해야 한다. 인도는 움직이기 전에 완벽한 예측 가능성을 필요로 하는 기업들을 위한 시장이 아니다. 인도는 잘 준비하고, 빠르게 적응하고, 진지하게 남을 수 있는 기업들을 위한 시장이다. ◆학생과 대중의 인식 학생과 미디어에 관한 논의에서 대중의 인식 문제가 다시 등장했다. 유럽 학생들이 인도의 노동 조건, 임금, 인권에 대해 비판적 질문을 자주 제기하면서도 유럽 상점에서 저가 패션을 구매하고 있다는 점이 지적됐다. 이러한 모순은 무역에 관한 논의가 얼마나 어려울 수 있는지를 보여준다. 소비자들은 윤리적 생산을 원하지만 저렴한 가격은 여전히 매력적이다. 학생, 기업가, 연사를 직접 만나게 함으로써 더 균형 잡힌 시각이 생길 수 있다. 목적은 비판을 없애는 것이 아니라 논의를 더 정직하게 만드는 것이다. 무역은 양측이 자신의 역할도 검토할 때만 공정하게 논의될 수 있다. 이는 구시대적인 유럽의 인도 이미지가 여전히 비즈니스 결정에 영향을 미치고 있기 때문에 중요하다. 유럽은 주로 인도를 빈곤, 아웃소싱, 저비용 생산을 통해 바라본다. 그 이미지는 불완전하고 갈수록 오해를 부른다. 그러나 인도는 또한 우주 프로그램이며 디지털 인프라 실험실이고 제약 강국이며 서비스 거인이고 제조 경쟁자이며 농업 문명이고 변화 중인 소비시장이다. 유럽은 인도에 대해 더 성숙한 시각이 필요하다. ◆브뤼셀의 역할 이번 회의 장소로 브뤼셀이 선택된 것은 우연이 아니었다. 이 도시는 유럽집행위원회, 유럽의회, 무역 대표부, 외교 네트워크, 기업 연합, 국제 자문 단체들과 가깝다. 인도 기업들에게 브뤼셀은 단지 벨기에의 수도가 아니다. 그것은 유럽 시장 접근을 형성하는 규칙이 준비되는 장소이기도 하다. 유럽 기업들에게 브뤼셀은 인도가 시장, 파트너, 생산기지로 어떻게 변화하고 있는지를 더 잘 이해할 수 있는 장소다. 그러나 브뤼셀은 최종 목적지가 아니다. 논의는 브뤼셀에서 뭄바이, 벵갈루루, 첸나이, 하이데라바드, 아마다바드, 푸네, 델리, 콜카타, 그리고 인도 경제생활의 많은 다른 중심지로 이동해야 한다. 유럽-인도 비즈니스 및 산업 센터(EICBI)는 인디아 살롱 브뤼셀의 기관 파트너였다. 그 참여는 모임에 분명한 비즈니스와 정책 차원을 부여했다. 회의실에는 상공회의소, 수출, 수입, 공공정책, 기술, 외교, 연구, 비즈니스 네트워크, 시장 진입 자문 경험을 가진 사람들이 모였다. 지난달 9일 오전에는 유럽의회에서도 회의가 열렸고 인디아 살롱 브뤼셀 모임에 앞서 유럽과 인도의 더 넓은 협력이 논의됐다. 하우툴스트 출신 시의원 요리스 힌드릭스는 그 오전 회의의 주목할 만한 손님이었다. 그의 참석은 EU-인도 논의가 수도, 외교 서비스, 대기업에 국한되지 않으며 지역 공직자와 지역 행위자들에게도 관련돼 있음을 보여줬다. ◆관세만이 아니다 회의의 핵심 메시지는 EU-인도 자유무역협정이 관세 인하로 축소돼서는 안 된다는 것이었다. 관세는 중요하지만 시장 접근의 한 부분일 뿐이다. 한 기업은 낮아진 관세의 혜택을 받을 수 있으면서도 잔류물 규정, 라벨링, 추적 가능성, 지속가능성 주장, 금융, 문화적 차이, 느린 의사결정에서 막힐 수 있다. 동시에 철저한 문서 관리, 좋은 관계, 신뢰할 수 있는 제품 품질을 갖춘 기업은 유럽의 엄격함을 장점으로 바꿀 수 있다. 인도 수출업체들에게 유럽은 어렵지만 가치 있는 시장일 수 있다. 유럽 기업들에게 인도는 거대하고 빠르게 변화하는 시장일 수 있다. 그러나 그들이 자신의 접근 방식을 조정할 의지가 있을 때만 그렇다. 바로 그 지점에서 한국과 일본과의 비교가 그토록 관련성을 갖는다. 그들의 가장 강한 기업들은 시장 접근을 법적 사건으로 대하지 않았다. 그들은 그것을 장기적인 사업 운영으로 대했다. 유럽도 그렇게 해야 한다. ⓒ천지일보 2026.07.06. (챗GPT) ◆EU가 韓日에서 배울 수 있는 것 일본에서 얻을 교훈은 인내, 산업 규율, 장기적인 제도적 후속 조치다. 한국에서 얻을 교훈은 속도, 소비자 밀착, 규모를 키울 용기다. 유럽에는 둘 다 필요하다. 일본으로부터 유럽은 단기적인 시장 주기가 아니라 30년 관계로 생각하는 법을 배울 수 있다. 현지 생산, 공급업체 개발, 연구개발, 인내심 있는 신뢰에 투자하는 법을 배울 수 있다. 인도는 자신의 강점을 잃지 않고 적응하는 기업에 보상한다는 점을 배울 수 있다. 한국으로부터 유럽은 브랜드 친숙도가 중요하고 서비스망이 중요하며 빠른 실행이 중요하다는 점을 배울 수 있다. 인도의 소비자들은 단순히 ‘프리미엄’이라는 가정만으로 접근할 수 없다. 그들은 서비스를 받아야 하고 답변을 받아야 하며 이해돼야 한다. 양쪽 모두로부터 유럽은 인도가 한 번에 진출되는 곳이 아니라는 것을 배울 수 있다. 인도에는 매일 진입해야 한다. ◆무역 문서 이면 브뤼셀의 메시지 인디아 살롱 브뤼셀의 가치는 EU-인도 협정을 제도적 언어에서 사업 현실로 끌어내렸다는 점에 있었다. 물론 관세는 중요하고 지속가능성은 중요하다. 지적재산권, 투자 보호, 조달, 서비스, 관세 절차 역시 중요하다. 하지만 진정한 핵심은 기업들이 이 협정을 실제로 활용할 수 있느냐는 점이다. 유럽 기업들이 인도를 이해하지 못하면 협정은 충분히 활용되지 못한 채 남을 것이다. 인도 기업들이 유럽을 이해하지 못하면 협정은 좌절감을 줄 것이다. 양측이 관계를 법적 문서로 축소한다면 그 아래에서 필요한 인간적·사업적 작업을 놓치게 될 것이다. 이것이 한국과 일본이 이 논의에서 중요한 이유다. 그들은 인도가 헌신에 보상한다는 것을 보여준다. 그들은 적응이 약점이 아니라는 것을 보여준다. 그들은 현지 존재가 글로벌 강점이 될 수 있음을 보여준다. 그들은 한 기업이 외국 기업으로 시작해 신뢰받는 기업이 될 수 있음을 보여준다. ◆인간적인 결과를 가진 협정 브뤼셀에서 EU-인도의 포괄적 자유무역협정(CEPA)은 궁극적으로 숫자를 훨씬 넘어서는 것으로 논의됐다. 그것은 생산 방식을 바꿔야 할 수도 있는 농민, 유럽 인증을 배워야 하는 기업가, 기회를 찾는 노동자, 국경을 넘어 이동하는 가족, 인도에 대한 시각을 조정하는 학생, 인도를 더 잘 이해하려는 벨기에 기업, 그리고 유럽을 단순한 단일 시장으로 취급해서는 안 된다는 사실을 깨닫는 인도 기업들과 관련된 문제다. 인디아 살롱 브뤼셀의 가치는 주요 정치적 이야기 아래의 그 실질적 층위에 있었다. 협정은 새로운 무역 흐름을 열 수 있지만 진짜 시험은 사람들이 그것을 실행할 수 있느냐다. 그래서 이 논의는 외교관과 무역 변호사들에게만 맡겨져서는 안 된다. 그것은 기업, 지방정부, 가족 기업, 농민, 대학, 상공회의소, 노동단체, 시민사회에도 속한다. 무역은 국경을 넘는 것에 관한 것만이 아니다. 이는 국경을 넘은 뒤 누가 누구를 이해하는가에 관한 것이기도 하다. ◆유럽의 선택 유럽은 이제 선택의 기로에 있다. EU-인도 협정을 외교적 성공으로 기념한 뒤 기업들이 인도의 광대하고 까다로운 시장을 스스로 헤쳐나가도록 둘 수 있다. 아니면 이 협정을 훨씬 더 깊은 경제적 학습 과정의 시작으로 대할 수 있다. 첫 번째 선택지는 보도자료만 만들어낼 것이다. 두 번째 선택지는 공장, 일자리, 연구 파트너십, 더 깨끗한 공급망, 더 강한 중소기업, 더 나은 농업 협력, 서비스 성장, 그리고 인도와의 더 균형 잡힌 관계를 만들어낼 수 있다. 유럽은 인도에 팔기 위해서만 가서는 안 된다. 유럽은 배우고 구축하고 머물기 위해 인도에 가야 한다. 그것이 인디아 살롱 브뤼셀에서 나온 더 깊은 사업적 교훈이었다. 인도는 유럽이 훈계를 들고 도착하는 것을 필요로 하지 않는다. 인도는 유럽이 진지함을 가지고 도착하는 것을 필요로 한다. 한국과 일본은 이미 그 길의 일부를 보여줬다. 이제 유럽은 인도를 방문하고 싶은 것인지 아니면 마침내 그곳에 정착할 것인지를 결정해야 한다.

item.title: [천지일보 이슈종합] 이병태 논란 끝에 사퇴·‘가짜뉴스 처벌법’ 시행·투표함 봉쇄 한 달·겨우 지킨 코스피 8000피·5년 이상 자영업자 폐업 역대 최다·청년미래적금 누적 234만명 신청·김민석 광주서 당권 출사표
item.content:encoded: [서울=뉴시스] 이병태 규제합리화위원회 부위원장이 15일 청와대에서 열린 규제합리화위원회 제1차 전체회의에서 발언하고 있다. [천지일보=김민철 기자] 이병태 대통령 직속 규제합리화위원회 부위원장이 “5.18 성역” 발언 논란으로 임명 약 3개월 만에 자리에서 물러났다. 온라인상에서 불법 및 허위조작정보의 확산을 막고 피해자를 보호하기 위해 마련된 개정 정보통신망법(가짜뉴스 처벌법)이 7일부터 본격적인 시행에 들어간다. 6.3 지방선거 투표용지 부족 사태로 서울 송파구 올림픽공원에서 시작된 ‘참정권 집회’가 한 달을 맞으면서 현장 분위기도 크게 달라졌다. 이외에도 천지일보는 지난 6일 주요 이슈를 모아봤다. ◆“5.18 성역” 발언부터 사퇴까지… 이병태 나흘 만에 낙마☞(원문보기) 이병태 대통령 직속 규제합리화위원회 부위원장이 “5.18 성역” 발언 논란으로 임명 약 3개월 만에 자리에서 물러났다. 배재고 야구부의 “스타벅스 가야지” 응원 논란을 두고 사회관계망서비스(SNS)에 올린 글이 정치권 공방으로 번진 데 이어 청와대의 공개 경고와 여권의 사퇴 요구가 잇따르면서 결국 자진 사퇴를 선택했다. 2026 북중미 월드컵 32강 탈락 이후 출범한 ‘K-축구 혁신위원회’가 대한축구협회 거버넌스 개혁을 최우선 과제로 제시했다. ◆‘가짜뉴스 처벌법’ 7일 시행… 허위정보 재유포 시 최대 10억☞ 온라인상에서 불법 및 허위조작정보의 확산을 막고 피해자를 보호하기 위해 마련된 개정 정보통신망법(가짜뉴스 처벌법)이 오는 7일부터 본격적인 시행에 들어간다. 이번 법 개정은 가짜뉴스로 인한 폐해가 속출하고 피해자가 양산되는 상황에서 조회수나 광고 수익을 가로채기 위해 허위 정보를 반복 생산하는 문제를 해결하고 건전한 온라인 환경을 조성하려는 취지에서 마련됐다. 제도 시행에 따라 네이버와 카카오를 비롯한 국내 대형 플랫폼사들도 이용약관 개정과 자율규제 가이드라인 수립 등 시스템 정비를 마친 상태다. [천지일보=남승우 기자] 6일 서울 송파구 올림픽파크텔에서 열린 K-축구 혁신위원회 출범식에서 공동위원장을 맡은 박지성 국제축구연맹(FIFA) 분과위원회 위원이 모두발언을 하고 있다. ⓒ천지일보 2026.07.06. ◆박지성 “신뢰 회복이 최우선”… “현행 협회장 선거제론 안 돼”☞ 2026 북중미 월드컵 32강 탈락 이후 출범한 ‘K-축구 혁신위원회’가 대한축구협회 거버넌스 개혁을 최우선 과제로 제시했다. 공동위원장을 맡은 박지성 국제축구연맹(FIFA) 분과위원회 위원은 “한국 축구가 팬들에게 잃어버린 신뢰를 회복하는 것이 혁신위의 가장 중요한 역할”이라며 협회장 선거 제도 개선과 축구 행정 혁신의 필요성을 강조했다. ◆[잠실 참정권 집회] 투표함 봉쇄 한 달… 구호·공간 분화 속 장기화☞ 6.3 지방선거 투표용지 부족 사태로 서울 송파구 올림픽공원에서 시작된 ‘참정권 집회’가 한 달을 맞으면서 현장 분위기도 크게 달라졌다. 초기에는 ‘재선거’ 요구가 중심을 이뤘지만 시간이 흐르면서 주장과 구호가 다양해지고 참가자들의 활동 구역도 점차 나뉘었다. 생수와 음식물을 나누던 단순 지원 공간에는 종교·언론·역사 관련 부스까지 들어섰고 의료와 법률 등 각종 자원봉사도 이어지면서 현장은 장기 체류형 집회 공간으로 변모했다. (서울=연합뉴스) 코스피가 상승 출발한 뒤 하락 전환해 8,000선을 겨우 지킨 6일 서울 중구 하나은행 딜링룸에서 직원이 업무를 보고 있다. 이날 코스피는 전장보다 37.01포인트(0.46%) 내린 8051.33에 마감했다. 2026.7.6 ◆코스피 ‘8천피’ 겨우 지켰다… 환율, 1530원으로 주간거래 마쳐☞ 6일 코스피가 약보합 마감했다. 한국거래소에 따르면 이날 코스피는 전장보다 37.01포인트(0.46%) 내린 8051.33로 마감했다. 코스피는 전장 대비 98.48포인트(1.22%) 오른 8186.82로 출발해 장중 한때 8327.26까지 뛰었다. 이후 하락 전환해 7815.53까지 밀렸다. ◆靑 “호남 반도체 클러스터 광주군공항 부지에 조성키로 결정”☞ 정부가 3대 메가 프로젝트의 하나로 추진하는 호남권 반도체 클러스터를 광주 군공항 부지에 조성하기로 했다. 강훈식 대통령 비서실장은 6일 청와대에서 열린 메가 프로젝트 민관 합동 점검회의 뒤 브리핑을 통해 “기업들은 호남권 입지 후보지 가운데 광주 군공항 부지가 가장 적합하다는 의견을 제시했다”며 이같이 밝혔다. 서울시가 자영업자 대상 ‘안심통장 2호’를 2000억원 규모로 출시하며, 청년창업자·노포사업자 등 취약계층 지원 조건을 완화해 오는 28일부터 신청을 받는다. 지난 달 30일 오전 중구 명동 지하상가의 한 매장에서 상인이 영업 준비를 하고 있다. ⓒ천지일보 2025.07.30 ◆창업 줄고 노포는 문 닫고… 5년 이상 자영업자 폐업 역대 최다☞ 5년 이상 영업한 자영업자들의 폐업이 역대 최대를 기록했다. 사업 부진으로 문을 닫는 사업자들이 절반을 차지하면서 금융위기 이후 가장 큰 비중을 차지했다. 건설 부진도 이어지며 건설사들의 말소·폐업 건수가 3년 연속 증가세를 이어간 것으로 나타났다. ◆배재고 “진심으로 반성”… 광주일고 “정정당당한 승부 펼치자”☞ 5.18민주화운동을 연상시키는 응원 구호로 물의를 빚은 서울 배재고등학교 야구부 학생 선수들이 광주제일고등학교를 찾아 공식 사과했다. 광주일고는 사과를 받아들이며 화해를 이뤄냈다. (서울=연합뉴스) 금융위원회는 29일부터 다음달 3일까지 출생연도와 관계없이 청년미래적금 가입신청을 받는다고 밝혔다. 가입신청 완료 후 다음달 6일부터 24일까지 자격을 심사하고, 서민금융진흥원에서 신청자에게 개별적으로 안내할 예정이다. 사진은 이날 서울 서울 중구 우리은행 본점 영업부에 청년미래적금 관련 안내문이 설치된 모습. 2026.6.29 ◆신청 마감된 청년미래적금… 누적 234만명 신청☞ 지난 3일 청년미래적금 가입 신청이 마감된 가운데 약 234만 3000명이 가입한 것으로 나타났다. 6일 금융권에 따르면 금융위원회와 서민금융진흥원은 지난달 22일부터 이달 3일까지 약 234만 3000명이 가입했다고 밝혔다. 가입 신청자 중 약 8만명은 소상공인 자격으로 가입을 신청했다. 연령별로는 30∼34세 청년의 가입 비중이 38.8%로 가장 높았다. 이어 25∼29세(36.5%), 19∼24세(24.7%) 순이었다. ◆김민석 광주서 당권 출사표… 정청래·송영길과 ‘3색 경쟁’☞ 김민석 전 국무총리가 6일 광주에서 더불어민주당 대표 선거 출마를 공식 선언하면서 8.17 전당대회를 향한 당권 경쟁이 본격화했다. 연임에 도전하는 정청래 전 대표와 출마 의사를 사실상 밝힌 송영길 의원도 각각 당의 정통성과 행정 경험을 내세우며 차별화에 나섰다. 김 전 총리는 이날 전남광주통합특별시 동구 전일빌딩245에서 기자회견을 열고 “이재명 정부 국정 성공에 대한 무한한 책임감을 위해 민주당 당대표 출마를 선언한다”고 밝혔다. 당권주자로 거론되는 인사 가운데 첫 공식 출마 선언이다.

item.title: [Brand Insight] Ottogi: Beyond a Good Company, Becoming a Strong Brand
item.content:encoded: [Cheonji Ilbo=Reporter Yu Youngsun] There is a brand that has been part of Korean dining tables for more than half a century. From its iconic yellow logo to curry, ketchup, ramen, and ready-to-eat meals, Ottogi’s products represent more than memories of a particular generation — they remain a familiar part of everyday life today. Founded in 1969, Ottogi has grown into one of Korea’s leading food companies by staying committed to its core value of providing high-quality food at reasonable prices, even in a rapidly changing food market. Ottogi founder and honorary chairman Ham Tae-ho established Poonglim Corporation in 1969 and introduced Korea’s first instant powdered curry, “Ottogi Curry.” At a time when curry was not commonly prepared at home, Ottogi made it possible for anyone to enjoy curry easily and conveniently. From the company’s early days, Ham emphasized the corporate philosophy of “contributing to the improvement of human dietary life through better quality, higher nutrition, and more advanced food products.” He believed that the essence of a food company was not simply selling products, but enriching people’s everyday meals. This philosophy has continued under second-generation leader Chairman Ham Young-joon. While maintaining the founder’s vision of creating “honest food and a trusted company,” Ham Young-joon has also pursued innovation in response to changing consumer trends. He has emphasized that a food company must remain faithful to quality while understanding changes in consumers’ lifestyles in order to earn long-term loyalty. Alongside strengthening its classic products, Ottogi has focused on new growth areas such as home meal replacements (HMR), premium products, online distribution, and global market expansion. In 2017, Ottogi gained significant public attention when it was invited to a business meeting at the Blue House during the Moon Jae-in administration — an unusual case for a mid-sized company. At the time, Ottogi was recognized for its consistent social contribution activities and its image of mutual growth. In particular, its long-running support program for children with heart disease, scholarship initiatives, and partnership-focused management style, which began during the founder’s era, received renewed attention. Consumers began calling the company “God-ttogi,” combining “God” with Ottogi, as a symbol of admiration. It reflected an era in which consumers evaluate not only products but also a company’s attitude and values. However, Ottogi’s greatest competitive strength ultimately comes from its products. Starting with Ottogi Curry, products such as tomato ketchup, mayonnaise, sesame oil, 3-Minute Meals, and Jin Ramen have become long-standing brands loved by consumers. Jin Ramen, in particular, has established itself as one of Korea’s representative ramen brands through continuous quality improvements and an accessible pricing strategy. Ottogi’s products have gained consumer trust not through extravagance, but through familiarity and consistency. The recent global popularity of K-food is creating new opportunities for Ottogi. As Korean cuisine becomes recognized worldwide as a form of cultural content, interest in Korean ramen, sauces, and convenient meal products continues to grow. Products such as Jin Ramen and various sauces are expanding their global presence by offering Korean flavors combined with convenience. A company that once focused on family dining tables in Korea is now evolving into a brand competing within the global food culture. Ottogi’s unchanging value lies in its identity as “a food company close to people’s everyday lives.” The honest product philosophy and consumer-centered approach emphasized by founder Ham Tae-ho remain at the heart of the brand. What continues to change, however, is the way those values are delivered. In response to the rise of single-person households, health-conscious consumption, diverse tastes, and the spread of global food culture, Ottogi continues to evolve its products and market strategies. The strength of a long-lasting brand lies in not remaining trapped in past success. A brand that is familiar but never outdated, a brand with a long history that continues to change — this is why Ottogi continues to hold a special place in consumers’ minds today.

item.title: [브랜드 인사이트] 오뚜기, 착한 기업을 넘어 강한 브랜드로
item.content:encoded: [천지일보=유영선 기자] 반세기가 넘는 시간 동안 한국인의 식탁을 지켜온 브랜드가 있다. 노란색 로고와 함께 떠오르는 카레, 케첩, 라면, 즉석식품은 특정 세대의 추억을 넘어 오늘의 일상 속에서도 계속 소비되고 있다. 1969년 창립한 오뚜기는 빠르게 변화하는 식품 시장 속에서도 ‘좋은 품질의 식품을 합리적인 가격에 제공한다’는 기본 가치를 지켜오며 한국 대표 식품 기업으로 성장했다. 오뚜기 창업주 함태호 명예회장은 1969년 풍림상사를 세우고 국내 최초 분말 즉석 카레인 ‘오뚜기 카레’를 선보였다. 당시만 해도 가정에서 쉽게 접하기 어려웠던 카레를 누구나 간편하게 즐길 수 있는 대중적인 음식으로 만든 것이다. 창업 초기부터 그는 “보다 좋은 품질, 보다 높은 영양, 보다 앞선 식품으로 인류 식생활 향상에 이바지한다”는 기업 이념을 강조했다. 식품 기업의 본질은 단순히 제품을 파는 것이 아니라 사람들의 식생활을 더 풍요롭게 만드는 데 있다는 믿음이었다. 이러한 철학은 2세 경영자인 함영준 회장에게 이어지고 있다. 함영준 회장은 창업주의 ‘정직한 식품, 신뢰받는 기업’이라는 방향성을 유지하면서도 변화하는 소비 환경에 맞춘 혁신을 추진해 왔다. 그는 식품 기업이 오래 사랑받기 위해서는 기본에 충실한 품질 관리와 함께 소비자의 생활 변화를 읽어야 한다고 강조해왔다. 전통적인 장수 제품의 경쟁력을 지키는 동시에 가정간편식(HMR), 프리미엄 제품, 온라인 유통, 글로벌 시장 확대 등 새로운 성장 영역에도 집중하고 있다. 2017년 문재인 정부 당시 청와대 기업인 간담회에 중견기업으로는 이례적으로 오뚜기가 초청되면서 사회적 관심이 커졌다. 당시 오뚜기는 꾸준한 사회공헌 활동과 상생 이미지로 주목받았다. 특히 창업주 시절부터 이어온 심장병 어린이 후원 사업, 장학 활동, 협력 관계를 중시하는 경영 방식 등이 재조명되며 소비자들은 오뚜기에 ‘God(갓)’을 붙인 ‘갓뚜기’라는 애칭을 사용하기 시작했다. 제품을 넘어 기업의 태도와 가치관까지 소비자가 평가하는 시대를 보여준 사례였다. 하지만 오뚜기의 가장 강력한 경쟁력은 결국 제품이다. 창립 제품인 오뚜기 카레를 비롯해 토마토케첩, 마요네스, 참기름, 3분 요리, 진라면 등은 오랜 기간 소비자 곁에 머문 대표 브랜드다. 특히 진라면은 꾸준한 품질 개선과 대중적인 가격 전략을 기반으로 국내 대표 라면 브랜드 중 하나로 자리 잡았다. 오뚜기의 제품들은 특별함보다 익숙함, 화려함보다 꾸준함을 무기로 소비자의 선택을 받아왔다. 최근 K푸드 열풍은 오뚜기에도 새로운 기회가 되고 있다. 한국 음식이 세계 시장에서 하나의 문화 콘텐츠로 소비되면서 라면, 소스, 간편식 제품에 대한 관심도 높아지고 있다. 진라면을 비롯한 라면류와 다양한 소스 제품은 한국적인 맛과 편리함을 앞세워 해외 소비자와 만나는 접점을 넓혀가고 있다. 과거 가족의 식탁을 책임지는 국내 브랜드였다면 이제는 글로벌 식문화 속에서 경쟁하는 브랜드로 변화하고 있는 것이다. 오뚜기의 변하지 않는 가치는 ‘사람들의 일상 가까이에 있는 식품 기업’이라는 정체성이다. 창업주 함태호 명예회장이 강조했던 정직한 제품 철학과 소비자 중심의 태도는 여전히 브랜드의 중심축으로 남아 있다. 반면 변화하는 부분은 그 가치를 전달하는 방식이다. 1인 가구 증가, 건강을 고려한 소비, 다양한 취향, 글로벌 식문화 확산에 맞춰 제품과 시장 전략은 계속 진화하고 있다. 오래 살아남는 브랜드의 힘은 과거의 성공에 머무르지 않는 데 있다. 익숙하지만 낡지 않은 브랜드, 오래됐지만 계속 변화하는 브랜드. 그것이 오늘날 오뚜기가 소비자의 마음속에 남아 있는 이유다.

item.title: ‘표현의 자유’ 논란 속 ‘개정 정보통신망법’ 오늘부터 시행
item.content:encoded: 24일 국회에서 열린 12월 임시국회 본회의에서 정보통신망법 개정안이 더불어민주당 주도로 처리되고 있다. 2025.12.24 (출처: 연합뉴스) [천지일보=김민철 기자] 온라인상 불법정보와 허위조작정보의 확산을 막기 위한 개정 정보통신망법이 7일 본격 시행됐다. 이른바 ‘가짜뉴스 처벌법’ 또는 ‘사이버렉카 근절법’으로 불리는 이번 법은 허위 정보를 반복적으로 유통해 피해를 키우고 조회수와 광고 수익을 얻는 행위에 무거운 경제적 책임을 묻는 내용을 담고 있다. 이번 개정은 온라인 공간에서 허위사실과 조작 콘텐츠가 빠르게 확산되면서 개인의 명예와 인격권 침해, 사회적 혼란, 경제적 피해가 잇따르고 있다는 문제의식에서 출발했다. 특히 자극적인 허위 정보를 생산·유통해 광고 수익을 얻는 일부 정보 게재자를 제재하고 피해자 구제 수단을 강화하겠다는 것이 입법 취지다. 제도 시행에 맞춰 네이버와 카카오 등 주요 플랫폼 사업자들도 관련 절차 정비에 나섰다. 이용약관을 개정하고 불법·허위조작정보 신고 접수와 처리 기준, 게시물 조치 절차 등을 마련하는 방식이다. 앞으로 이용자는 대규모 플랫폼에 올라온 게시물에 대해 불법정보 또는 허위조작정보라고 판단할 경우 신고할 수 있다. 개정안의 핵심은 악의적 허위조작정보 유통자에 대한 경제적 제재 강화다. 고의 또는 중대한 과실로 허위조작정보를 정보통신망에 유통해 타인에게 손해를 입히거나 부당한 이익을 얻은 경우 법원은 실제 손해액의 최대 5배까지 배상하도록 할 수 있다. 기존의 게시물 삭제나 형사처벌 중심 대응에서 나아가 허위정보 유통으로 얻은 수익 구조 자체를 억제하겠다는 취지다. 판사봉. (출처: 연합뉴스) 가중 손해배상 대상은 일정한 영향력과 수익성을 갖춘 정보 게재자다. 직전 3개월 동안 3건 이상의 정보를 게재해 광고 등으로 수익을 얻은 사람 가운데 구독자 수가 10만명 이상이거나 직전 3개월간 월평균 조회수가 10만회 이상인 경우 등이 포함된다. 유튜버를 비롯한 사회관계망서비스(SNS) 채널 운영자, 온라인 콘텐츠 생산자, 일부 언론사 채널 등이 적용 대상에 들어갈 수 있다. 최대 10억원의 과징금도 도입됐다. 다만 과징금은 플랫폼 사업자가 아니라 법원에서 불법·허위조작정보로 확정된 정보를 반복적으로 다시 유통한 정보 게재자에게 부과된다. 사실이나 의견을 불특정 다수에게 전달하는 것을 업으로 하는 사람이 직전 3개월간 3건 이상의 정보를 올려 수익을 얻고 법원에서 불법·허위조작정보로 판결이 확정된 내용을 2회 이상 재유통한 경우가 대상이다. 과징금은 위반 행위의 중대성, 반복성, 피해 규모 등을 고려해 산정된다. 기준 금액을 정한 뒤 가중·감경 절차를 거쳐 최종 부과액이 결정되는 구조다. 허위사실 적시에 따른 명예훼손죄의 벌금 상한도 기존 5000만원에서 7000만원으로 높아졌다. 플랫폼의 역할도 커진다. 앞으로 네이버, 카카오, 유튜브 등 대규모 정보통신서비스 제공자가 운영하는 플랫폼에 올라온 게시물에 대해 누구든지 불법·허위조작정보 신고를 할 수 있다. 신고를 받은 플랫폼은 자체 정책에 따라 삭제, 차단, 표시 제한 등 필요한 조치를 검토하고 그 결과를 신고자와 게시자에게 알려야 한다. [천지일보=박준성 기자] 국민의힘 장동혁 대표가 6일 서울 여의도 국회에서 열린 최고위원회의에 참석해 있다. 장 대표와 최고위원들은 내일부터 시행되는 개정 정보통신망법의 부당함을 알리기 위해 검은색 마스크를 썼다고 밝혔다.ⓒ천지일보 2026.07.06. 다만 언론사가 플랫폼을 통해 게재한 기사나 자료는 삭제 등 조치 대상에서 제외된다. 그러나 언론사가 별도로 운영하는 SNS 채널이나 영상 플랫폼 계정에 올라온 게시물은 사안에 따라 적용 대상이 될 가능성이 있다. 이에 따라 법 시행 이후 언론 보도와 온라인 콘텐츠, SNS 게시물의 경계가 어디까지인지도 쟁점이 될 전망이다. 허위조작정보 여부를 누가 어떤 기준으로 판단할지도 논란이다. 개정법은 허위정보와 조작정보를 규정하고 있지만 실제 적용 과정에서는 ‘공공의 이익 침해’, ‘현저한 훼손’ 등 표현의 해석을 두고 다툼이 생길 수 있다. 단순한 의견 표명이나 정치적 주장, 풍자와 패러디는 규제 대상에서 제외된다는 설명이 나오지만 시행 초기에는 신고와 분쟁이 늘어날 수 있다는 관측도 제기된다. 플랫폼이 신고 게시물을 보수적으로 처리할 가능성도 우려된다. 짧은 시간 안에 허위 여부를 명확히 판단하기 어려운 만큼 플랫폼이 법적 책임과 논란을 피하기 위해 일단 삭제하거나 노출을 제한하는 방식으로 대응할 수 있다는 것이다. 이 경우 허위정보 피해를 막겠다는 제도가 오히려 표현의 자유를 위축시킬 수 있다는 지적이 나온다. 언론 보도에 대한 전략적 봉쇄소송 우려도 남아 있다. 비판 보도나 의혹 제기의 대상이 된 기업, 정치인, 권력기관 등이 승소 가능성과 별개로 거액의 손해배상 소송을 제기해 보도 자체를 위축시킬 수 있다는 문제다. 정부와 여당은 공익 목적의 정당한 비판과 감시 활동은 보호된다는 입장이지만 실제 소송 부담만으로도 언론과 콘텐츠 생산자가 위축될 수 있다는 반론이 적지 않다. 개정법에는 공공의 이익을 위한 정당한 비판과 감시 활동을 방해하려는 목적의 손해배상 청구에 대해 법원이 신속히 각하할 수 있는 절차도 포함됐다. 하지만 해당 장치가 실제로 얼마나 효과적으로 작동할지는 지켜봐야 한다는 의견이 제기된다. 법원이 충분한 심리 없이 소송을 걸러내는 데 부담을 느낄 수 있고 제도가 자리 잡기 전까지는 당사자 간 법적 다툼이 이어질 가능성이 크기 때문이다. 사실확인 절차의 독립성도 과제로 꼽힌다. 플랫폼은 자체 판단이 어려운 경우 외부 사실확인 단체의 검증을 활용할 수 있지만 관련 기관 지원 구조를 놓고 국가 개입 가능성을 우려하는 목소리도 나온다.

item.title: Europe must learn to land in India before it can trade with India
item.content:encoded: Andy Vermaut is the EU Climate Pact Ambassador and a leading voice in global diplomacy and human rights advocacy. As President of the World Council for Public Diplomacy, European Community House, and Fundamental Rights Movement (Postversa), he has exposed human rights abuses from Sudan to Iran. With over 20 years as an award-winning investigative journalist, he has uncovered systemic failures through data-driven storytelling. A sought-after keynote speaker at the UN and global summits, he bridges climate urgency with human rights accountability. Guided by his conviction that “Climate crimes are human rights violations,” Vermaut reframes ecological crises as legal imperatives, calling for reparations for the most vulnerable. ⓒ천지일보 2025.08.17. BRUSSELS – The EU-India debate is often described in the language of trade: tariff lines, market access, rules of origin, customs procedures, sustainability clauses and investment protection. But at India Salon Brussels, held on Tuesday 9 June 2026 at Novotel Brussels Off Grand Place, the most important message was not hidden in the legal architecture of the Comprehensive Free Trade Agreement. It was much more practical. Europe can sign a trade agreement with India, but that does not mean European companies automatically know how to do business in India. That distinction matters. The European Union and India are preparing a far-reaching economic relationship that goes well beyond the lowering of customs duties. It concerns goods, services, investment, intellectual property, standards, sustainability, supply chains, labour mobility and strategic economic cooperation. Yet the Brussels discussion made clear that a signed agreement is only the beginning. The real question is whether companies, investors, regions and entrepreneurs on both sides know how to turn such an agreement into working economic reality. At India Salon Brussels, one lesson stood out sharply: Europe should look much more carefully at how Japan and South Korea have built their presence in India. Their approach has not been perfect and has not been free of difficulties. But Japanese and Korean companies have often understood something that European companies still underestimate. India is not a market that can be entered from a distance. India is a country where companies have to land, stay, adapt, localise and build trust over time. India is not a spreadsheet market Many European companies still look at India through reports, statistics, policy papers and trade missions. They see a country of nearly 1.5 billion people, a fast-growing consumer base, high demand for infrastructure, digital services, clean technology, machinery, food products, pharmaceuticals and mobility solutions. They see opportunity. But too often, they do not yet see India itself. That was one of the strongest undercurrents of the India Salon discussion. India cannot be understood only from Brussels, Paris, Berlin, Amsterdam or Milan. It cannot be managed only through email, PowerPoint decks, export brochures or short visits. A company may understand the tariff schedule and still fail in India. A company may have the right product and still fail because it chooses the wrong state, the wrong partner, the wrong sales model, the wrong price point, the wrong speed of decision-making or the wrong cultural assumptions. Japan and Korea learned this earlier. Their strongest companies did not treat India merely as an export destination. They built factories, dealer networks, supplier ecosystems, after-sales structures, local management layers and long-term brand familiarity. They made India part of their global industrial map. Suzuki’s Indian story is one of the clearest examples. Maruti Udyog and Suzuki signed their licence and joint venture agreement in 1982, and the Maruti 800 reached the Indian market in 1983. Over time, Maruti Suzuki became far more than a carmaker selling Japanese technology in India. It became part of India’s own automotive history. Suzuki itself later described Maruti Suzuki as one of the most successful joint projects between India and Japan. That is the first lesson for Europe. India rewards companies that embed themselves. It is much less forgiving for companies that want quick market access without long-term presence. Japan understood patience as a business method Japanese companies often move slowly, but once they move, they often build for decades. That is precisely what matters in India. The India-Japan commercial relationship did not begin yesterday. Panasonic already established a manufacturing presence in India decades ago, followed later by Suzuki, Denso and other Japanese industrial players. The India-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, which came into effect in 2011, covers goods, services, movement of natural persons, investment, intellectual property, customs procedures and other trade-related fields. This matters because Japan did not build its Indian position through one agreement alone. It built it through accumulated presence. Industrial cooperation, manufacturing, supplier training, local employment, research and development, quality systems, patient capital and repeated government-business dialogue all played a role. Japan has also increased its administrative and diplomatic attention to India. The creation of a dedicated Japan-India Economic Affairs Division by the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs underlines how seriously Tokyo now treats the economic relationship with New Delhi. India is not just another market file. It is becoming a strategic economic file in its own right. Europe should pay attention. The EU has strong trade negotiators and excellent regulatory capacity, but business follow-through is often fragmented between EU institutions, Member States, chambers of commerce, regional agencies, private consultants and sector bodies. India does not need another European brochure. It needs European continuity. 나렌드라 모디 인도 총리와 스즈키자동차 오사무 스즈키 회장이 2022년 8월 인도 간디나가르에서 열린 스즈키 마루티의 인도 파트너십 40주년 기념 행사에서 손을 흔들고 있다. (출처: 뉴시스) The Suzuki lesson: localisation is not a slogan At India Salon Brussels, participants referred to examples such as Maruti Suzuki and Toyota to show that successful business in India requires more than selling into India. It requires adjusting to India. The Suzuki story is powerful because it shows how a foreign company can become local without disappearing into the local market. Maruti Suzuki did not simply import Japanese cars. It worked with Indian conditions, Indian roads, Indian consumers, Indian price sensitivity and Indian industrial development. The result was a brand that helped shape India’s mass automobile market. In 2022, Maruti Suzuki commemorated 40 years of Suzuki’s partnership with India. During that ceremony, Suzuki announced a new R&D centre in India, intended to strengthen research capabilities for India and global markets. That is not just production. That is knowledge transfer, engineering, talent development and confidence in Indian technical capacity. Europe should draw a direct lesson from this. If European companies only see India as a place to sell finished products, they will remain vulnerable. If they see India as a place to design, test, adapt, produce and scale, their position changes. India is not only a demand market. It is also an innovation market. It has engineers, software developers, industrial clusters, family businesses, skilled technicians, agricultural knowledge, pharmaceutical capacity, textile traditions, digital public infrastructure and a population that can test products at enormous scale. A European product that works in India may later work in Africa, Southeast Asia, the Middle East or Latin America. A European product that cannot survive India’s price sensitivity, infrastructure gaps, climatic conditions and regional diversity may not be as globally competitive as its maker believes. Korea understood speed, scale and consumer intimacy South Korea followed a different path from Japan, but its lesson is equally important. Korean companies often combine rapid execution with heavy localisation, strong branding and aggressive consumer proximity. Samsung, Hyundai and LG are not marginal players in India. They are deeply visible in daily life: mobile phones, televisions, refrigerators, cars, service centres, showrooms and advertising. They did not become familiar to Indian consumers by waiting for perfect market conditions. They invested, expanded, adapted and kept selling. Samsung’s Noida factory is a clear symbol of this approach. The factory, set up in 1996, became one of Samsung’s key electronics manufacturing facilities in India. In 2018, Samsung inaugurated a major expansion and described the Noida plant as the world’s largest mobile factory, with capacity planned to double from 68 million to 120 million mobile phones a year. Samsung also stressed that it had entered India in 1995 and built factories, R&D centres, a design centre, retail networks and customer service points across the country. That is not remote exporting. That is industrial occupation in the positive economic sense: being physically present, visible, accessible and accountable. Hyundai offers another lesson. Hyundai entered India in 1996 and has since developed India into one of its major global manufacturing and export bases. Its more recent investment plans show that India is no longer viewed merely as an emerging consumer market, but as a production, research and export hub. Europe should not copy Korea blindly. But it should understand the strategic principle. Korea does not only ask how to export to India. Korea asks how to become part of India’s consumption, production and service landscape. The Korean CEPA lesson: agreements need industrial follow-up India and South Korea already have their own Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. It came into effect in 2010 and covers trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights and investment. India and Korea have continued to discuss improvements and updates, including goods, services, rules of origin, investment and sanitary and phytosanitary standards. This is important for Europe because it shows that trade agreements are not static trophies. They need maintenance. They create disputes. They expose imbalances. They require review, sectoral correction and political patience. The EU-India agreement will be no different. European companies should not imagine that once the agreement enters into force, India will suddenly become easy. There will still be customs questions, certification questions, data questions, sustainability questions, labour questions, regional differences and administrative friction. Korean companies did not avoid all of that. They built through it. Europe must do the same. It must prepare companies not only to enter India, but to survive the second, third and fourth year. The first year is often curiosity. The later years reveal whether the strategy is real. 2024년 9월 24일 인도 첸나이 외곽 스리페룸부두르에 있는 삼성 공장. (출처: 뉴시스) Europe is strong in rules, but India asks for relationships Europe’s great strength is regulation. The EU can set standards that reach far beyond its borders because access to the European market requires compliance with European rules. That was also discussed at India Salon Brussels. Sustainability, reporting, traceability, pesticide residues, green claims, supply-chain documentation and labour conditions are now part of trade reality. This gives Europe power. But it can also create arrogance. For Indian businesses, Europe can look like a maze of standards, audits, certificates and slow replies. For European businesses, India can look unpredictable, informal and difficult to read. Both perceptions contain some truth. But neither is sufficient. Japan and Korea show that companies succeed when they translate rules into relationships. They build local teams that understand the administration. They create service networks that understand the consumer. They train suppliers. They invest in people who can move between headquarters and Indian realities. They accept that India cannot be reduced to one national operating model. The EU-India agreement contains opportunities for exporters, service providers, investors, agricultural producers, technology firms and industrial manufacturers. But even the best agreement will not replace trust. A reduced tariff can open a door. It cannot build a market. India is federal, regional and deeply diverse One of the recurring points in the Brussels discussion was that India is not one single market. That sentence is often repeated, but not always taken seriously. India’s states differ in language, infrastructure, political culture, food habits, consumer behaviour, purchasing power, industrial policy, labour availability and administrative practice. A European company that enters Maharashtra may have a very different experience from one that enters Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala or West Bengal. Japan and Korea often learned this through physical presence. Their companies built plants in specific locations, developed regional supplier bases and adapted products to local expectations. Europe often starts from a macro-view: India as one country, one market, one growth story. That is too abstract. Europe must learn to choose India state by state, sector by sector and partner by partner. This is especially important for small and medium-sized European companies. A large multinational can absorb mistakes. An SME cannot. For many European SMEs, India should not begin with a national strategy. It should begin with one state, one reliable partner, one product, one compliance pathway and one clear customer segment. That may sound modest. In India, it is often the only serious way to start. The after-sales lesson European companies often underestimate after-sales service in India. They focus on product quality, technology and brand reputation. But in India, service accessibility can decide whether a product survives. Korean consumer brands understood this very well. Samsung’s communication about India stressed not only manufacturing, but also retail outlets and customer service points across the country. That is a business lesson, not a marketing detail. In a market as large and varied as India, trust is built after the sale. Can the product be repaired? Is there a local contact? Are spare parts available? Does the warranty mean something? Does the company answer? Is the brand visible in smaller cities? Can the family trust it? Can the business buyer rely on it when something breaks? European companies that enter India with premium products but weak service networks risk becoming niche suppliers for a small urban elite. That may be profitable in some sectors, but it is not an India strategy. Japan and Korea often built networks before Europe finished analysing risk. Local management is not optional Another lesson from Japan and Korea is the role of local management. European companies often send expatriates to India with limited preparation, limited family support and limited authority. They expect them to “manage India” while key decisions remain in Europe. That rarely works. India requires local decision-making. It also requires trust in Indian managers. Companies that keep India as a subordinate sales territory will not understand the speed of the market. Companies that allow Indian leadership to shape product, pricing, distribution, hiring and communication stand a much better chance. Hyundai’s appointment of Tarun Garg as the first Indian CEO of Hyundai Motor India was symbolically important in this regard. It showed that a long-established foreign company in India can move from expatriate-led presence to deeper local leadership. Europe should take that seriously. If European firms want India to become central to their global growth, Indian executives must be central to their decision-making. India’s middle class is not Europe’s middle class One of the traps for European companies is to misread India’s consumer base. India has wealth, aspiration and a rapidly changing urban economy. But it also has extreme price sensitivity, uneven income growth and enormous differences between metropolitan consumers and smaller-town or rural consumers. Japanese and Korean companies often adapted to this reality by offering products designed for Indian price points, Indian family use and Indian infrastructure conditions. This does not mean lowering quality. It means redesigning value. Europe sometimes struggles with this. A European company may think its brand justifies a premium. In India, that premium must be earned daily. Consumers may respect European quality, but they will still compare price, service, durability, availability and social proof. The Indian consumer is not waiting passively for Europe. The Indian consumer already has Indian, Korean, Japanese, American and Chinese options. In many sectors, Europe is arriving late. Sustainability must become practical The India Salon debate also showed that sustainability is becoming one of the main gateways to the European market. This is not limited to large corporations. Smaller suppliers can be pulled into reporting requirements because their larger clients need data on emissions, origins, labour conditions and environmental impact. For Indian exporters, this is difficult but also strategic. A company that can document its chain, prove its claims, manage residues, trace inputs and verify labour practices can gain an advantage in Europe. A company that treats sustainability as marketing language will face growing risk. Europe can help here, but only if it avoids preaching. Indian producers need practical pathways: affordable certification, clear documentation, cooperative training, technology transfer, testing capacity and predictable demand. The question is not whether European standards matter. They do. The question is whether Europe can help partners meet them without turning compliance into a wall. Japan and Korea are useful examples because they often think in ecosystems. They train suppliers. They build industrial clusters. They support quality improvement. Europe must bring the same ecosystem thinking to sustainability. Agriculture will test the agreement Agriculture was one of the most concrete parts of the Brussels discussion. Mangoes, spices, moringa, natural farming, organic products, pesticide residues and traceability all came up. The lesson was simple: a product may be attractive, but access to Europe depends on the chain behind it. This is where the EU-India agreement will face real-world pressure. Europe wants safe food, credible green claims and protection for sensitive sectors. India wants opportunity for its producers, farmers and exporters. Both positions are legitimate. But a trade agreement will only work if it creates practical bridges between them. If an Indian producer wants to sell organic or residue-free products to Europe, the surrounding farming environment may matter. If neighbouring fields use pesticides, contamination risks may arise. That means export readiness is not only an individual company issue. It can become a village, district or regional organisation issue. Europe should not underestimate this. It should work with India on testing infrastructure, farmer training, cooperative models, local incentives and traceability tools. Otherwise, agricultural opportunity will remain limited to a small number of well-organised exporters. Moringa as a practical example During the Brussels discussion, moringa became one of the most concrete examples of how European market access works in practice. A producer who wants to bring moringa to Europe cannot only focus on yield, packaging or price. The product must also be documented, tested and credible. If it is presented as organic or residue-free, the production environment must support that claim. That means the farmer’s own field is not enough. The wider area matters. If neighbouring farms use pesticides, contamination risks can remain. If water sources are polluted, that can affect the product. If transport, storage or processing are poorly documented, the commercial story weakens. This is where trade becomes local development. To export to Europe, a producer may need to convince neighbouring farmers, organise training, create common standards, invest in testing, build traceability and secure better prices. A European customer buying moringa may therefore be influencing not only one producer, but an entire farming zone. That is the kind of practical economic cooperation that the EU-India agreement should support. Natural farming and new rural income The discussion also touched on natural farming, soil quality, water protection and possible additional income streams for rural areas. Hemp was mentioned as a plant with deep roots that can store carbon in the soil and may also help in the context of polluted land. The idea of certified carbon storage as a possible source of income was discussed, alongside broader questions about natural methods and environmental restoration. There were also ideas about microplastics in water and possible natural techniques to bind or address them. Such ideas require further study and verification, but their presence in the discussion showed that EU-India cooperation does not need to be limited to export volumes. It can also involve agricultural knowledge, soil restoration, water quality, biodiversity and rural development. This is another area where Europe can learn from India. India has centuries of agricultural knowledge, local experimentation and low-cost adaptation. Europe has strong scientific institutions, regulatory systems and market demand for verifiable sustainability. If these strengths are combined correctly, the result can be more than trade. It can become applied cooperation. Labour mobility is also trade policy At India Salon Brussels, labour mobility was not treated as a separate migration issue. It was part of the economic conversation. That is the right approach. Trade is not only goods crossing borders. It is people building confidence. Indian professionals in Europe can help European companies understand India. European entrepreneurs in India can help build new partnerships. Students, engineers, technicians, advisers and families become part of the bridge. Japan and Korea have used people, training and company culture as part of their India strategy. Europe must do the same, but in a way that respects rights, family life and social protection. Belgium and other European countries face labour shortages in several sectors. India has skills, ambition and a young workforce. But mobility must not become exploitation. If Europe wants Indian talent, it must offer clear rules, fair treatment and real inclusion. Otherwise, it will lose credibility. The same applies in reverse. European companies sending people to India must prepare them properly. India is not only different in the office. It is different in housing, schooling, traffic, family expectations, bureaucracy, food, climate, social rhythm and support networks. Failed expatriation is not always a business failure. Often it is a family failure that the company failed to anticipate. Culture also determines whether trade works The Brussels meeting repeatedly moved beyond tariffs and rules. Cultural differences were seen as at least as important. India and Europe were discussed as two large civilisational spaces with long histories, many languages, regional differences and strong internal diversity. India was not viewed only as a nation state, but also as a society with deep historical layers, religious influences, family networks and local identities. Europe also has its own cultural and political history, shaped by humanism, individual rights, privacy, the rule of law and regulation. This comparison helped clarify that companies do not only exchange products. They also bring expectations with them. If those expectations are not understood, misunderstandings become more likely. One cultural contribution focused on the difference between the European emphasis on the individual and the Indian emphasis on embedded responsibility. The concept of dharma was used to describe how a person in India is often seen within a wider web of obligations towards family, profession, country and society. This differs from the European tradition, where individual rights, personal choice, privacy and autonomy are more central. These differences do not have to block cooperation, but they must be understood.
